theme: 3 terms on sharing one object: a type that shares its instances, checking for the same object, and a protocol only classes can adopt

terms.definition: A type whose instances are shared, so copying a variable gives you a second name for the same object.
terms.example: `Player` is a Reference Type, so updating `copy` also updated `original`.

terms.definition: An operator, written as three equals signs, that checks if two references point to the same object.
terms.example: Use the Identity Operator to check it's the same `Player`, not just an equal one.

terms.definition: A protocol that every class conforms to automatically, so you can use it to allow only class instances.
terms.example: I added AnyObject to `Listener`, so structs can't adopt it anymore.

video.title: Reference Type, Identity Operator & AnyObject | Day 37
video.description:
Learn to explain how classes share one object in Swift: Reference Type, Identity Operator & AnyObject, with real code, a quiz at the end and each example read twice (normal, then slow).

Today's terms
Reference Type - A type whose instances are shared, so copying a variable gives you a second name for the same object.
Identity Operator - An operator, written as three equals signs, that checks if two references point to the same object.
AnyObject - A protocol that every class conforms to automatically, so you can use it to allow only class instances.

Quiz at the end - write your answers in the comments, then watch again to check.

landscape.hook: Can you explain these class terms in English?

dialogue.title: Why did first change too?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Jake, I changed `second.score`, and `first.score` changed too. Is that a bug?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Not a bug. `Player` is a class, so it's a Reference Type.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: No. With a Reference Type, both names point to one object.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: How can I check that in code?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Use the Identity Operator, three equals signs. It prints true here.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Two equals signs compare values. The Identity Operator compares objects.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: OK. And why does `ScoreListener` say AnyObject?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: AnyObject means only classes can adopt it, so a struct can't.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Makes sense. So only a Reference Type fits there.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Exactly. AnyObject for class-only protocols, the Identity Operator for same-object checks.
A Reference Type shares one object between names.
